newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway to clamp down on some securities trade.
newsitem.headline: Norway to clamp down on some securities trade.

text.p: Norway's government proposed new restrictions on Friday on trading in securities by brokers and institutional investors on the Norwegian market.

"We must have rules and regulations which ensure that the interests of clients are looked after in a satisfactory way and which stop individuals from using their position to obtain advantages they are not entitled to," Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg told a news conference.

Norwegian politicians and media have been up in arms recently over what they call "a culture of greed" in the financial community following a controversy over a share issue in a small offshore company that went public in January.
Under the proposal by the Labour minority government, employees in unit trusts must commit themselves to keeping for at least 12 months any stock they buy for personal gain.

The law already applies to brokerage staff, but the proposal contained general suggestions for brokerages and financial institutions to adopt stricter internal rules for employees trading for personal gain.
The government proposal said any private trade by staff in such institutions must be reported by the employer to the Norwegian Banking, Insurance and Securities Commission.

Two weeks ago an investment executive in Norway's biggest insurance company Storebrand ASA quit because he felt persecuted by media questioning in a controversy over alleged trading by portfolio managers for personal gain.

Riulf Rustad, executive vice president of Storebrand Investment Management, which manages the group's securities portfolio, said he had not in any way tried to enrich himself through his position in Storebrand.
His announcement followed the resignation of Storebrand Spar investment manager Tore Schoeitz. He left after the Storebrand management said it no longer had confidence in him.

The row began with a share issue administered by Platou Securities in Norwegian Applied Technology (NAT). The issue was oversubscribed 13 times and the price eventually rose 150 percent from the original level of 6.50 crowns.
Several portfolio managers in insurance companies were given the opportunity to buy stock while hundreds of other investors were allegedly shut out from the issue.
